#3093. Trusted AI Governance Starts Where Intent Becomes Action

CTO at WSO2, Inc., humanizing tech and architecting transformation; author & keynote speaker; advocating distributed, agentic systems.

​Most enterprise AI governance conversations still start with the model. Accuracy, safety, bias, explainability and output reviews dominate the discussion. But now, those concerns are no longer enough.

In the agentic era, AI systems are not just generating answers. They are calling tools, invoking APIs, retrieving data, delegating work and taking action inside business processes.

Now, the enterprise also has to determine whether the agent was allowed to take a specific action, under the right authority, with the right context, through the right tool, at the right time and for the right purpose. Trusted AI governance starts where intent becomes action.

Traditional enterprise governance assumes software behavior can be specified before deployment. A service exposes an API contract. A workflow follows a defined sequence. A release can be reviewed, tested and approved before it goes live. Runtime governance usually confirms that the system continues to behave according to what was already specified.

Agentic systems do not fit that model cleanly. An agent can reason over context, call tools, retrieve data, invoke APIs, delegate tasks and decide when to continue, stop, escalate or retry. The output matters, but the path matters, too. The authority used, data accessed, tools called and decision to act all become part of the governed surface.

That creates an inversion. In deterministic systems, governance can start with the output specification. In agentic systems, the enterprise must govern the boundary where intent becomes action and retain evidence after the action. Pre-deployment review still has value, but there is no final output contract that can be verified once and trusted forever.

A model can be powerful, accurate and useful. That does not make it trusted in an enterprise. Trust comes from the architecture around the model, including controls that make agent behavior inspectable, attributable and bounded.

Inspectable means the enterprise can see what happened, including tool calls, data access, applied policies, human oversight and resulting action. Attributable means the enterprise knows who or what acted, and under whose authority. An agent should not act as an anonymous workload or shared service account. It needs identity, delegated authority and traceable actions.

Bounded means the agent operates within defined limits: access, tools, data, policy, cost, jurisdiction and human approval. Without these properties, trust collapses into hope.

Trusted AI governance requires two complementary enforcement models: inline governance and infrastructure-enforced governance.

Inline governance is implemented inside the agent or application flow. Teams add policy checks, validation logic, safety rules, approval steps and logging directly into the system. This matters because it has access to local workflow context, business intent and domain-specific rules.

But inline governance is not sufficient by itself. In a large enterprise, every team implementing its own governance logic creates uneven coverage. Controls get duplicated, drift over time and become hard to audit consistently.

Infrastructure-enforced governance applies controls outside the agent implementation through gateways, proxies, runtimes, service meshes, identity systems, model gateways, API gateways and other enforcement points. This gives the enterprise a common enforcement layer at shared boundaries for model calls, API calls, tool access, data access and agent-to-agent traffic.

The two models are not substitutes. Inline governance gives domain precision. Infrastructure-enforced governance gives enterprise consistency. One without the other becomes fragmented or too coarse.

Authorization is essential, but it is not the same as safety. An agent may be authorized to use an email tool, but that does not mean every email it writes should be sent. It may include confidential information, make an unapproved commitment or send a message to the wrong recipient.

The risk is rarely in the tool name alone. The risk is in the parameters of the action, such as which customer record, which amount, which recipient, which query, which file, which authority and which purpose. Authorization determines access to a capability. Safety determines whether a specific use is acceptable in context.

Agents also need identity. Many enterprise systems still depend on shared service accounts, user sessions and embedded credentials that are difficult to attribute cleanly. That model becomes dangerous when agents take multistep actions. The enterprise needs to know who the agent is and on whose authority it is acting.

For technology, AI and security leaders, the priority is to make governance executable, not to write another AI policy document.

Start with discovery. You cannot govern agents, tools, models, APIs, delegated authorities or agent-to-agent interactions you cannot see.

Then treat agents as first-class actors. Give them identities, make delegation explicit, and avoid hiding agentic behavior behind anonymous workloads or shared accounts. Define the boundaries where intent becomes action, such as the points where agents reach models, APIs, tools, data, workflows and other agents. Combine inline and infrastructure-enforced controls at those boundaries, and capture evidence after action.

The agentic era will not be governed by policy documents alone. Governance has to be designed before deployment, enforced while agents act and proven after action through evidence. Design-time governance defines policies, tools, evaluations and approval paths. Runtime governance enforces boundaries when agents access systems, use tools, invoke APIs, delegate work and coordinate with other agents.

Evidence closes the loop. Without evidence, governance becomes a claim. With evidence, it becomes something the enterprise can inspect, audit and improve. The enterprises that get this right will not simply “trust AI.” They will build systems where trust is inspectable, attributable and bounded by design.​

#3092. Acumen Pharmaceuticals: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

A single confirmatory Phase III trial design could streamline the path to regulatory approval if November data validates the oligomer-targeting approach.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 26, 2026, Acumen Pharmaceuticals (ABOS -7.72%) confirmed that it expects to report top-line Phase II trial results for its lead Alzheimer's drug candidate, sabirnetug, in November 2026. The readout represents the first major clinical test of whether targeting toxic protein clusters called amyloid beta oligomers in the brain slows cognitive decline. For long-term investors, positive Phase II data could validate this central scientific thesis and establish a direct path toward a single confirmatory Phase III registration trial. Three key takeaways from the call highlight what investors need to know.

Acumen is preparing top-line Phase II results for sabirnetug, its proprietary monoclonal antibody designed to neutralize toxic amyloid-beta oligomers rather than clear established plaque. The Phase II trial evaluates two doses against placebo across 18 months, tracking primary cognitive endpoints alongside imaging and fluid biomarkers.

The business finished the third quarter with $79 million in cash and marketable securities, which are liquid short-term investments. This balance provides a financial bridge past the upcoming clinical readout and funds planned research and development into early 2027 without immediate dilution pressure.

Preclinical work on Acumen's enhanced brain delivery (EBD) platform demonstrated improved antibody penetration across the blood-brain barrier, a biological filter that limits drug absorption into brain tissue. Lead candidate ACU-401 generated up to a 40-fold increase in exposure in the frontal cortex of nonhuman primates while preserving oligomer selectivity, paving the way for planned investigational new drug regulatory filings for human clinical testing in mid-2027.

Clinical momentum is accelerating ahead of the November readout, and the pipeline is moving steadily toward its next regulatory stages. Acumen holds key structural advantages through its specialized oligomer-targeting antibodies and a planned single confirmatory Phase III trial design. To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.

#3089. ​Houston, We Have A Communications Problem: Why Silence After A Breach Is Killing Trust

By Ian Weisberger, co-founder and CEO of CoinRoutes.

In financial services, 2026 has been the year of the constant cyberattack. Whether it is wealth managers losing clients’ Social Security numbers to stolen logins, employees tricked into revealing customer data or botnets hammering firms with AI-generated password attempts, these threats are hitting companies on a near-weekly basis.

With AI making attacks easier, the pace is unlikely to slow. Financial services companies understand that breaches are becoming a fact of life. What they cannot accept, though, is being left in the dark. In financial services, especially in fintech and fast-growing areas such as decentralized finance, communication after a breach has too often been lacking.

​To understand the problem, it’s worth starting with what good looks like. In September, Revolut was reported to have suffered a data breach involving fraudulent government data requests. The firm acknowledged the incident, said it had contacted affected customers directly and described steps it took to block the fraudulent requests and notify relevant authorities.

Later that month, when Bitget reportedly suffered a hack involving more than $350 million, CEO Gracy Chen publicly addressed the impact, explaining the withdrawal suspension and stating that the company would cover the losses.

Neither company had every answer at the outset, but these examples illustrate an important principle of incident communications: acknowledge what is known, explain what remains uncertain and give customers clear information about the steps being taken. That approach can help preserve trust even when the full picture is still emerging.​​

Not every incident is accompanied by the information clients need to understand the risks. A few weeks ago, we began receiving questions about a cyberattack involving a portfolio management service provider we work with. Our systems were not affected, but we share several clients with the provider, leaving us with questions we could not yet answer.

At the time of writing, we were still seeking details about the incident, including what information may have been exposed and how the attackers gained access. Although the provider had indicated that it would share a post-incident review, we did not yet have the information needed to address our clients’ concerns.

Many clients came to us looking for answers, and we had concerns that trading histories and portfolio data could have been exposed. For a trading firm, that can be enough to work out its strategies, among the most valuable things it owns. We asked for details that would have put those concerns to rest, but they did not arrive.​

In financial services, a provider’s clients can collectively manage hundreds of billions of dollars, and they have their own obligations to investors, shareholders and regulators. If providers cannot explain what data was taken, they cannot tell their own clients, and one firm’s silence puts everyone in a difficult position.

This matters most in the newer corners of finance. Sectors such as decentralized finance are still earning the trust of businesses and consumers, with far less reputation to fall back on than an established bank. When something goes wrong, silence costs them more than anyone.

In our own operations, we’ve made timely incident reporting a contractual obligation, committing to investigate incidents and provide clients with a post-mortem within 24 to 48 hours. Because we run a trading system around the clock, we write one even for five-minute outages. For consumer-facing businesses, I would expect a first message closer to an hour. The principle is simple: Say what you know, admit what you don’t yet know and come back as soon as you know more.

As an industry, we need to agree on what accountability looks like and stop pretending breaches don’t happen. At a minimum, every firm should commit to acknowledging breaches within hours, keeping open lines with key partners and providing continuous updates until the picture is complete.

Holding providers accountable starts before anything goes wrong. These are the questions I’d ask any technology provider handling your data before a breach occurs:

1. If something goes wrong, when will I first hear from you? Not when the investigation is finished, but when you first tell me there is a problem, followed by regular updates as the picture becomes clearer.

2. What exactly will you tell me? Telling me it has been fixed is not enough. I want to know what was taken, how it happened, what has changed and whether it could happen again. Above all, I want to know what the stolen information now allows someone to do.

3. If I ask whether my data was affected, can you give me a straight answer? When one of our clients had a messaging account phished, we pulled the IP addresses that had accessed their account with us, traced what had happened and gave them a clear answer. That is the standard I expect.

4. How are passwords, API keys and other secrets protected? Sensitive credentials should be protected through appropriate key-management systems, with access tightly restricted and unnecessary exposure in application memory minimized. Ask whether keys are protected by dedicated key-management hardware or an equivalent, and who has access.

5. If someone gets into one client’s account, can they reach anyone else’s? Each client’s data and credentials should be kept separate, and logins, credentials, trading and client-facing services should be walled off from one another, so that if one area is compromised, the damage stops there.

6. What can someone do with a stolen key, login or access token? Credentials do get stolen. What matters is how much access they provide, how long it stays valid, whether its use would be detected and whether connections are restricted to approved IP addresses. Stolen customer read-only keys should not allow the attacker to access funds or other clients’ information.

When I first came into this industry in 2017, what attracted me was its openness and the competitive energy that came with it. Today, that openness matters more than ever. As cyberattacks become more sophisticated and easier to carry out, breaches will keep happening, and no firm can promise they won’t. What every firm can promise is to communicate honestly and quickly when they do.​

Management plans to use third-party financing structures rather than draining internal cash to fund large vehicle fleets, with Uber anticipating 700 AVs on its network by year-end, and growing to 2,000 in 2027.

Fuel cost inflation and shifting immigration dynamics restricted the supply of available drivers in key international ride-hailing markets like Brazil and India. Management reallocated marketplace incentives to restore driver capacity heading into the peak holiday season.

Following recent expansion agreements, management is pulling back on mergers and acquisitions (M&A), or corporate buyouts, to integrate existing platforms. Capital allocation will prioritize organic growth, AV expansion, and share buybacks, or the repurchasing of company stock.

Network effects across mobility (Uber’s ride-hailing business) and food delivery drive consumer retention, while high vehicle utilization gives the platform a structural cost advantage over stand-alone autonomous fleets. #3081. Why Individual AI Gains Don’t Add Up To Company Value

Dr. Son Nguyen is Orient Software’s CTO & co-founded Neurond AI, companies specializing in software development, AI, & data science services

​A few months ago, I asked our DevOps and finance teams the same question: What does it cost us each month to run the cloud infrastructure for one of our larger projects? Using different AI tools and data, they returned with different answers.

I couldn’t tell which answer to trust, where the information came from, whether it was current and whether correcting it would help others.

Now, imagine this across thousands of employees and AI tools.

Individual productivity is clearly improving with AI. A Gallup survey from May 2026 found that 65% of employees at organizations that have implemented AI reported a positive effect on their productivity and efficiency.​

But do thousands of assistants, each holding its own fragment of context, add up to a smarter company? I don’t think it necessarily does. While individual AI use can make each employee faster, only a company brain makes the company smarter.

McKinsey’s August 2026 report on the state of AI found that 89% of organizations are now using AI, and 80% of respondents say AI has improved their individual productivity. However, only 37% attribute at least some earnings before interest and taxes impact to AI, which was unchanged over the previous year.

We have become quite good at giving employees access to AI, but what happens to everything they learn from using it?

Each AI chat is its own island. Employees ask questions, refine answers and share business context. Yet that learning often stays within one interaction or workflow, and the next employee starts from scratch.

MIT’s NANDA initiative calls this the “learning gap.” Its preliminary study of 52 organizations found that most enterprise AI systems struggle to retain feedback, adapt or improve over time. The result? Thousands of employees become more productive without the organization becoming proportionally smarter.

Based on my experience, four issues explain why personal gains rarely become organizational gains:

1. Knowledge is scattered and often leaves with people. An employee develops a useful prompt, workflow or understanding of a customer issue, but that knowledge rarely becomes part of the company’s shared memory.

2. Companies lack a shared definition of what their information means. Without it, AI spreads existing inconsistencies faster.

3. Answers lack evidence. If AI doesn’t show the source of the information, it can produce an answer that sounds right without giving the organization a reliable basis for acting on it.

4. There is no shared learning loop. An employee discovers that an AI answer is wrong and corrects it, but that correction stays in their conversation. The next person can encounter the same error.

This is why I believe the quality of the underlying system matters at least as much as the model’s intelligence.

The BEAVER benchmark found that state-of-the-art AI agent frameworks using GPT-5.2 scored only 10.8% on questions drawn from real private data warehouses. As I discussed in my earlier article on AI system design, the model is only one layer. The surrounding architecture determines how information is retrieved, interpreted, governed and used.

A smarter model does not automatically create a smarter company.

Companies need a system that can turn individual interactions into shared organizational intelligence. I call this a company brain. The goal is to make organizational knowledge usable in decision-making. ​

A company brain is neither a chatbot on top of a data lake nor traditional knowledge management. It is not an off-the-shelf product or a platform project.

Instead, it is an operating model. Vendors can provide technology, but cannot decide what information is authoritative, who can access it or who is accountable when AI gets something wrong. When one person learns something valuable, that knowledge should become available to the right people and AI systems, with appropriate governance and evidence.

Before calling an AI system a company brain, I would test it against five requirements.

• Evidence: Every answer should show its source, owner and last update. I’ve explained before why every AI agent decision requires strong evidence. Without evidence, an AI answer may be useful, but not accountable. This matters most in regulated work, where every figure must be traceable. For high-risk uses such as hiring, credit and education, the EU AI Act requires high-quality data and traceability logs from December 2, 2027, for any company offering such systems in the EU. For those uses, the evidence standard is about to become a compliance standard.

• Meaning: Departments must share consistent definitions. If sales and finance mean different things by “revenue,” connecting their data won’t resolve the inconsistency.

• Permissions: People and AI agents should access only what they’re authorized to see and do, especially as AI moves from answering questions to taking actions.

• Learning: When an error is corrected once, the correction should improve the system for everyone. Outdated knowledge should also have a way to expire rather than remain available forever.

• Ownership: Someone at the executive level must own the outcome, with a dedicated budget and clear accountability. Otherwise, a company brain risks becoming everyone’s priority but nobody’s responsibility.

You don’t need a platform decision to begin building the brain. Start with questions your sales, finance, operations, customer success or engineering teams need to answer every week.

Measure how long it takes to get a trustworthy answer with a verifiable source, owner and date. Call this your time to trusted answers.

Then ask: Who corrects errors? Does that learning reach others? Can AI agents act safely within their permissions? These questions reveal more about AI maturity than license counts or daily usage.

To achieve success with enterprise AI, turning what one person learns into organizational intelligence is more important than making individuals faster. Your job isn’t to ask which model to buy, but what your AI knows about your company, and whether it can prove it.

VTI has a long track record. This fund was established in May 2001. Over the past 25 years, it's delivered average annual returns of 9.38%. Future returns are not guaranteed, but let's assume that you could earn that same return for the next 25 years or more.

If you invested $400 a month in the VTI, earning 9.38% annualized returns, in five years, your investment would grow to $28,945. After 10 years, you'd have $74,262. After 20 years, you'd have $256,293. After 30 years, you'd have $702,488. And in year 34, you'd pass the million-dollar mark -- your investment would now be worth about $1.028 million.

What if VTI can deliver stronger returns and get you to millionaire status faster? Over the past five years, this fund has delivered 10.95% annualized returns.

Let's assume you invested $400 per month in VTI and the fund maintained its 10.95% average annual return. After 10 years, you'd have $80,073. After 20 years, you'd have $306,410. After 30 years, you'd have $946,190. And in year 31 you'd become a millionaire, with more than $1.05 million.

Over the past 10 years, VTI delivered even stronger annualized returns: 14.87%. There's no guarantee that such a strong return will keep coming forever. But let's assume you can earn that higher return on your VTI investments -- this rate of return could make you a millionaire even faster.

If you invested $400 a month in VTI, earning an average annual return of 14.87%, after 10 years you'd have $96,841. After 20 years, you'd have $484,211. And after 25 years of investing in VTI, you'd be a millionaire: $1,000,709.

#3079. Colgate-Palmolive vs. Hershey: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is the Better Buy for 2027?

Both of these defensive stocks are growing sales about 6%, but one offers a higher yield and a lower valuation as cocoa costs weigh on its shares.

Defensive investors often look for stable dividends and household names during times of market uncertainty. Choosing between Colgate-Palmolive (CL +3.28%) and Hershey (HSY +4.15%) requires understanding their different approaches to global growth and category dominance.

Colgate-Palmolive offers broad international exposure through its leadership in oral care and pet nutrition. Hershey provides a concentrated bet on the resilient American snacking market with its portfolio of iconic chocolate brands. Comparing these two giants helps reveal which better aligns with your strategy for 2027.

Colgate-Palmolive is a global leader in oral care and hygiene, operating as one of the most recognizable names among consumer staples stocks. The company sells essential products like toothpaste and soaps in over 200 countries and relies on its Hill's Pet Nutrition segment for significant growth.

On a trailing 12-month basis through the September quarter, revenue reached $21 billion, representing roughly 6% year-over-year growth. Net income was $2 billion. This level of profitability reflects the steady global demand for the company's diverse portfolio of household and personal care brands.

As of its September 2026 balance sheet, the company carried a debt-to-equity ratio of 12x, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity. Its current ratio was about 1x, measuring the company's ability to pay short-term obligations with its current assets.

TTM free cash flow was nearly $3.8 billion, representing cash generated after accounting for all capital expenditures.

Hershey is a snacking powerhouse with a portfolio of more than 70 brands, including iconic sweets, mints, and chocolate products. The company primarily focuses on its North American confection and snacking segments while gradually expanding its international presence in regions like Brazil. McLane Company represents roughly 27% of consolidated net sales as a primary distributor for retail chains, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

TTM revenue for the September quarter was $12.2 billion, an increase of 6.7% over the year-ago period. Net income was nearly $1.8 billion. This performance highlights the company's ability to maintain sales growth and consumer loyalty in the highly competitive snack market.

The debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 1.1x, calculated by dividing total debt by the value of shareholder equity. The current ratio was roughly 1.2x, indicating the company's ability to meet short-term liabilities with its short-term assets. TTM free cash flow was close to $2.1 billion.

Colgate-Palmolive faces risks from international macroeconomic and geopolitical instability, particularly regarding its operations in Ukraine and volatile markets like Venezuela. The company also deals with intense global competition from private labels and must navigate substantial litigation risks related to talc claims. Furthermore, its reliance on a limited number of single-source suppliers for key raw materials could impact production.

Hershey faces volatility in global commodity markets, especially cocoa, which has weighed on its results over the last few years. The company is currently working through international growth challenges and the integration of acquisitions like LesserEvil. Additionally, it must manage technology risks associated with its global ERP system and potential cyber threats.

Hershey currently offers a more attractive valuation based on its lower Forward P/E and its lower P/S ratio, which compares the price to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

I would buy Hershey because it offers more value than Colgate shares. Hershey has faced record-high cocoa prices in recent years, which has sent its stock down and dividend yield up. It offers a higher yield at 3.4% compared to Colgate's 2.2% as of Nov. 4, 2026.

That higher yield is also well supported by free cash flow, with Hershey distributing about 55% of its free cash flow over the past year. By comparison, Colgate paid out 44% of its trailing free cash flow. Both are healthy payout ratios that provide ample cushion to sustain and grow the dividend even if profits weaken due to a recession.

Colgate is the leader in toothpaste and owns other household brands, including Hill's pet food. This drives stable sales in almost any economy, but I don't believe people are going to lose their taste for chocolate either. Hershey's revenues have grown for many years, reflecting a strategy to expand its portfolio of candy and snacks, including Skinny Pop. These brands put it in a solid position for long-term growth.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

#3070. The Future Of AI Will Be Decided In The Physical World

Daisuke Okanohara is CEO of Matlantis Coporation, and Co-founder and CTO of Preferred Networks, Inc.

​Every conversation about the future of AI circles back to the same assumptions: bigger models, more data, more compute. We treat progress as a contest of intelligence. Yet the constraint that will decide how far AI goes over the next decade has little to do with intelligence and a great deal to do with physics.​

AI is running into two physical walls that no amount of clever software can talk its way past.

In a modern AI system, far more energy goes into moving data around than into performing the calculations themselves. The calculations inside a chip are remarkably cheap. The real expense lies in shuttling enormous volumes of data between memory and processor, billions of times every second. By some engineering estimates, that movement can consume ten to a hundred times more energy than the computation it serves.​

For two decades, processing power has raced ahead while the speed of feeding data to it has crawled, and today’s large language models are limited less by how fast they can think than by how fast they can be fed.​

The bill lands on the balance sheet and on the power grid. Running the AI we expect to deploy across the economy could require tens of gigawatts of additional electricity. The ceiling on AI’s growth is becoming an energy ceiling, and that energy is spent in a place few people think to look: the distance data must travel.

The second wall sits one level deeper, in the materials our hardware is built from.​

Better chips, better batteries, better energy systems: nearly every hardware advance the AI era depends on eventually comes down to discovering or improving a material. Materials discovery has always been agonizingly slow. The number of possible combinations is effectively limitless, while the number humanity has tested remains vanishingly small.​

That mattered less when hardware progress had room to run elsewhere. It matters enormously now, because materials are precisely where both walls have to be broken: new architectures to shorten the distance data travels, new materials to move electricity with less waste, new chemistries to store energy more densely.

The instinct is to spend through these walls, buying more chips and standing up more data centers. That buys time without changing the trajectory, because it keeps optimizing the very designs that created the bottleneck.​

The more durable path is using AI to redesign the physical layers beneath AI itself.​

For most of computing history, those layers were designed in isolation. Materials scientists handed properties to device engineers, who handed components to chip designers, who handed hardware to system builders. When the binding constraints are physical and cut across every layer, the layers have to be designed together. Having spent years building both AI chips and the AI tools that design materials, I see this cross-layer approach as the defining shift of the coming decade.​

Three changes follow in practice. Organizationally, teams that once optimized their own slice hold a shared goal and work across team boundaries, so a system-level question like halving energy per query gets answered partly at the materials level. In process, sequential handoffs become joint development, with materials treated as design variables from the start and simulation as a standard gate before capital commits to hardware. In budget, funding follows the genuine bottleneck on the path to the goal.​

Materials discovery is where this change is furthest along. Understanding how a material behaves once meant either a physical experiment or a simulation too slow to model anything realistic. AI has broken that trade-off by learning the rules of how atoms interact, reaching near-laboratory accuracy at speeds that were recently impossible. At Matlantis, we have watched work that would once have demanded roughly 20 years of conventional calculation finish in about a week. Companies, including Volkswagen and Panasonic, now use this kind of simulation to explore materials at a pace no traditional lab could match.​

Speed of that magnitude changes decisions by moving materials questions earlier. Screen candidates in parallel with product design instead of ahead of it. Verify early whether materials that are scarce, regulated, or exposed to supply chain risk can be replaced, and whether promising but untested ones hold up. Make go or no-go roadmap calls on simulation evidence in weeks instead of lab evidence in years.

Picture where this leads. AI agents survey the research, propose candidate materials and run thousands of simulations in parallel around the clock, sending only the rare promising candidate to an automated lab for physical confirmation. The bottleneck shifts from human hours to the genuine limits of physics and experiment, a far better problem to have.​

Leaders can prepare now with three moves. First, build an in-house team that can read AI results critically, because the value of ten thousand simulations depends on the judgment applied to the ten that matter. Second, restructure the development cycle around that speed, with simulation running from day one rather than after prototypes exist. Third, choose partners that span layers: the suppliers, foundries and research institutions that own the parts of the stack you don’t.​

A caveat: even far more capable AI will never fully solve the physical world, because reality holds layers of complexity that cannot be predicted from the rules beneath them. The useful question is where irreversibility begins. Trust AI to explore, rank and explain at a scale humans cannot. Reserve for humans every decision that cannot be undone: synthesizing a material, committing capital, taking a product to market. Experiment keeps the final word. AI changes how fast and how intelligently we can run it.​

The decisive edge over the next decade will belong to whomever understands that AI’s progress now runs through the physical world, and who designs across every layer of the stack rather than optimizing a single one. Where physics sets the limit, AI is becoming the way through.​

This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

A significant drop is eye-catching, but bear in mind that you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. Since September, mortgage rates have been hovering around 7%. That’s a full percentage point higher than they were at the beginning of 2026.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.43% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3067. ASML vs. Marvell Technology: Which Artificial Intelligence Stock Is a Better Buy Going into 2027?

ASML's near-monopoly on chipmaking lithography and Marvell's AI data push sit on very different rungs of the industry, and their valuations and risks tell divergent stories.

The race for better artificial intelligence continues to reshape the market, making investors choose between equipment giants and chip designers. Should you buy ASML (ASML -3.60%) or Marvell Technology (MRVL -7.08%) today?

ASML provides the complex lithography systems used by the world's leading foundries to print the most advanced microchips. Marvell specializes in infrastructure solutions, connecting and moving massive amounts of data across cloud and carrier networks. Both companies are pivotal to the future of semiconductor technology, but they occupy very different rungs on the industry ladder.

ASML manufactures the lithography systems that are essential for the production of advanced microchips found in everything from smartphones to data centers. It is currently the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, notes are critical for cost-effective microchip scaling. The company serves the global semiconductor stocks ecosystem by delivering hardware and software for EUV and cheaper deep ultraviolet (DUV) applications.

In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached $36.7 billion, representing a growth of 15.6% compared with the prior fiscal year. This expansion in the top line helped the company generate a net income of $10.8 billion. The net margin, which measures the percentage of revenue remaining after all expenses are paid, reached 29.4% during this period.

According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.2x shows the company uses very little borrowed money relative to its equity. The current ratio of approximately 1.3x indicates it maintains sufficient short-term assets to cover immediate liabilities. Free cash flow, which is the cash left over after accounting for capital expenditures, reached $12.4 billion for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025.

Marvell Technology designs data infrastructure solutions that power artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and automotive industrial end markets across the globe. The company reported in its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, that its revenue is highly concentrated among a limited number of buyers. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as one distributor represented nearly 37% of revenue and a single direct customer accounted for roughly 14%.

In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached $8.2 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 42.1%. This sharp increase in sales helped the company achieve a net income of $2.7 billion. The net margin for the period reached 32.6%, reflecting a significant improvement compared with the losses reported in the prior fiscal year.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.3x indicates a healthy balance between debt and equity. The current ratio of approximately 2.0x measures its ability to cover short-term obligations, and free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, was nearly $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 33.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

ASML faces potential volatility in the global chip market, where cycles of high demand for new equipment can be followed by periods of overcapacity. Geopolitical tensions also pose a significant threat, as trade restrictions on high-end lithography equipment can limit sales to certain geographic regions. Additionally, the extreme complexity of its machines means any production delays or technical hurdles in next-generation systems could impact its long-term growth trajectory.

Marvell Technology faces risks from significant revenue concentration, as a few large customers account for a majority of its annual sales. Strategic and integration risks are heightened by large-scale acquisitions, notably the announced $115 billion all-stock acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE -7.85%). Additionally, the company faces intense competition from Broadcom (AVGO -2.00%) and potential supply chain disruptions due to the geographic concentration of its manufacturing partners.

ASML appears more affordably valued based on its Forward P/E and its P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

ASML and Marvell Technology are both great stocks to own for exposure to the artificial intelligence boom. The former is an attractive AI stock since it holds a legal monopoly over the EUV lithography machines needed to construct AI chips, as competitors have not been able to successfully replicate the technology at scale. However, if I had to choose between these two, I would invest in Marvell.

Not only did Marvell report 42% year-over-year revenue growth in its 2026 fiscal year (FY), in its Investor Day held on Oct. 6, management set a FY 2031 target of $70 billion to $90 billion in sales. That's incredible growth compared to FY 2026's $8.2 billion, and indicates the company is seeing strong customer demand for its AI solutions.

That's where Marvell's bid to acquire Lumentum comes in. Lumentum reported fiscal Q1 revenue of $1.3 billion on Nov. 2, which represents a jaw-dropping 137% year-over-year increase. Its optical connectivity offerings enable rapid data transmission, a critical feature for data-hungry AI systems.

Marvell's acquisition caused its share price to fall, as Wall Street weighed the dilution risk of the all-stock deal. This creates an opportunity to pick up Marvell shares on the dip, as I believe Marvell's addition of Lumentum makes the company stronger over the long run.

Robert Izquierdo has positions in ASML, Broadcom, and Marvell Technology. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends ASML, Broadcom, Lumentum, and Marvell Technology. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3065. Geron Corp (GERN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

First profit as a commercial-stage biotech, on RYTELO growth and cost cuts.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Geron Corporation (GERN +16.13%) reported its first quarter of profitability since its transition to a commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company, supported by RYTELO adoption and reduced operating expenses. Management stated that the company is focused on deepening its penetration into the U.S. community oncology market, where it sees thousands of additional eligible patients. The company confirmed its full-year revenue targets while lowering expense projections following a strategic workforce reduction implemented in late 2025. Strategic priorities now include evaluating business development opportunities to expand the hematology pipeline following the discontinuation of the Phase 3 IMpactMF trial.

Operator: Hello, and welcome to the Geron Corporation Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the call over to Dawn Schottlandt, SVP, Investor Relations and Corporate Affairs. You may begin.

Dawn Schottlandt: Good morning, everyone. Welcome to the Geron Corporation Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Before we begin, please note that during the course of presentation and question-and-answer session, we will be making forward-looking statements regarding future events, performance, plans, expectations and other projections, including those related to our 2026 financial guidance, our current RYTELO commercialization strategy and related opportunities in the U.S. and the EU, the therapy potential of RYTELO, other anticipated clinical and commercial events and related time lines, the sufficiency of our financial resources and other statements that are not historical fact, which, of course, involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual events, performance and results to differ materially from those contained in these forward-looking statements.

Therefore, I refer you to the risks and uncertainties described in today's earnings release under the heading Risk Factors in Geron's most recent periodic report filed with the SEC, which identify important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in these forward-looking statements and future updates to Geron's risks and uncertainties, disclosures, including in its upcoming quarterly report on Form 10-Q. Geron undertakes no duty or obligation to update its forward-looking statements. Joining me on today's call are several members of Geron's management team; Harout Semerjian, Chief Executive Officer; Ahmed ElNawawi, our Chief Commercial Officer; Dr. Joseph Eid, Executive Vice President, Research and Development and Chief Medical Officer; and Michelle Robertson, our Chief Financial Officer.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Harout to discuss Geron's progress in the third quarter.

Harout Semerjian: Thank you, Dawn, and good morning, everyone. We continue to execute our strategy to build a leading hematology company. We're delivering consistent RYTELO demand growth, reinforcing our confidence in the low-risk MDS U.S. commercial opportunity and RYTELO's growth trajectory over the next several years. We also initiated a gated commercial launch in targeted European markets that gives us the optionality to scale up RYTELO's availability through partnerships. Last week, we announced the discontinuation of the IMpactMF trial evaluating imetelstat in relapsed and refractory myelofibrosis following a recommendation by the independent DMC. We believe this is the right course of action for patients and for Geron.

In the third quarter, we continued to see increased prescribing from community practices leading to a quarter-over-quarter demand growth of 10% and net revenue growth of 5% or $60.1 million. This represents a 27% increase in net revenue year-over-year. This performance keeps us on track to achieve the mid- to high end of our full year 2026 net revenue guidance range of $220 million to $240 million and reinforces our confidence that RYTELO has a long growth runway in the U.S. This year, we started executing our ex U.S. go-to-market commercial strategy, focused on addressing unmet patient needs and broadening access to RYTELO while prioritizing U.S. price integrity.

Recent developments, including the exclusion of orphan drugs like RYTELO from the CMS GLOBE model gives us the opportunity to serve more patients globally. We initiated a gated commercial launch to make RYTELO available in targeted European markets, beginning with Germany, where RYTELO is expected to be commercially available by the end of this year. In Europe, our approach enables us to retain strategic control of pricing without having to establish full infrastructure in each market or commit to a large upfront investment. This hybrid model also allows us to remain flexible and open to partnership opportunities.

To support our global reach, we recently increased our engagement and presentations at multiple international medical meetings, and we're encouraged by the interest from hematologists in key markets. We will continue to explore opportunities in other geographies where we believe we can help address the significant unmet need of low-risk MDS patients. As we continue to strengthen our operations, another area of focus for us is financial discipline where our investments are intentional and targeted. Our operating expenses were down 9% year-to-date compared to the prior year reflecting our continued focus on operational efficiency. This discipline is enabling us to update our full year 2026 total operating expense guidance range from $220 million to $230 million.

With $339 million of cash on hand, we have a strong balance sheet to fund our current operations which gives us flexibility to pursue business development opportunities. With that, I'll turn it over to ElNawawi to provide more detail on RYTELO's commercial performance and our execution.

Ahmed ElNawawi: Thank you, Harout. We are pleased to report our fourth consecutive quarter of demand growth for RYTELO, reinforcing the need for this drug and its potential long-term value as a preferred treatment in second-line low-risk MDS. In the third quarter, we achieved a 10% demand growth for RYTELO compared to the second quarter of this year, an 8% increase in prescribing accounts, predominantly from community practices expanding our footprint to more than 1,700 accounts since launch. With first and second-line patient starts on a rolling 12-month basis at 36%.

We believe that RYTELO has the potential to deliver consistent quarter-over-quarter growth for years to come, driven in large part by continued adoption in the community setting where there are still thousands of patients that can benefit from RYTELO. Our focus is on accelerating that adoption through targeted personal and nonpersonal engagements that reinforce RYTELO's differentiated clinical efficacy in second-line low-risk MDS patients while continuously educating hem/oncs on dosing and management of cytopenias. RYTELO's unique mode of action as a first-in-class telomerase inhibitor. It's broad label and position in NCCN guideline provide a strong foundation to drive durable long-term growth. Turning to our efforts in Europe.

We've taken a gated operational approach where we drive regulatory engagement and local reimbursement process to ensure RYTELO reaches the appropriate patients at a price that reflects unique value. Our model allows us to broaden RYTELO's access with a staged upfront investment while preserving flexibility for the future. We have already initiated our launch in Europe and plan to make RYTELO commercially available in Germany by the end of the year with plans to follow in 2027. We are encouraged by the interest we're seeing across markets, supported by investigated experience with imetelstat and the significant unmet need in low-risk MDS. I now turn it over to Joe to discuss our medical and scientific engagement efforts.

Joseph Eid: Thanks, ElNawawi. Last week, we announced our decision to discontinue the Phase III IMpactMF trial evaluating imetelstat and JAK inhibitor in relapsed/refractory myelofibrosis. This decision was based on the recommendation from the independent data monitoring committee informing us that the trial was unlikely to meet its primary endpoint of overall survival. Importantly, there were no known safety signals observed in the trial that changed the known safety profile of imetelstat. We are committed to unblinding the data, conducting a detailed analysis of this rich data set and sharing findings at an upcoming medical meeting that may help inform future research.

We are deeply grateful to the patients and families as well as the investigators and clinical teams whose dedication made this research possible. Turning to low-risk MDS. This quarter, we presented at leading hematology meetings, both global and regional further communicating the growing body of evidence supporting RYTELO's differentiated profile, including evidence of disease-modifying activity. Just as importantly, these meetings created meaningful opportunities to engage directly with the medical community, exchange insights and deepen scientific dialogue around the evolving treatment of low-risk MDS. At SOHO, we continue to build strong momentum through impactful data presentations, sponsored dedication and broad KOL engagement powered by a coordinated full team approach.

Our low-risk MDS real-world evidence poster showed meaningful hemoglobin improvement with imetelstat despite short treatment duration and later on used in U.S. community oncology practice in the immediate post-launch period. This marked the second real-world evidence presentation this year adding to the growing body of evidence that reinforces findings from our Phase III IMerge trial and the safety, efficacy and tolerability profile of RYTELO. Additional data presented at the 88th Annual Meeting of the Japanese Society of Hematology and the 2026 Annual Meeting of the German, Austrian and Swiss Societies for Hematology and Medical Oncology further highlighted the durable clinical outcomes observed within imetelstat and expanded the growing body of evidence supporting its differentiated profile.

Across the presentations, Phase III IMerge findings and real-world experience reinforce the durability and clinical relevance of treatment outcomes, including findings suggesting that treatment-emergent cytopenia may reflect an on-target effect associated with meaningful clinical outcomes, such as hemoglobin improvement and transfusion independence in low-risk MDS. Importantly, the presentations also demonstrated growing scientific interest and investigator experience with imetelstat outside the U.S. as we continue to deepen engagement with the global hematology community. Beyond congress presentations, we continue to strengthen the scientific foundation of RYTELO through 2 manuscripts published in peer-reviewed journals, further expanding the body of evidence supporting imetelstat's role in low-risk MDS and its potential to address significant unmet need.

Looking ahead, the 68th ASH Annual Meeting in December will provide another opportunity to build on this body of evidence with new data across low-risk MDS and other hematological diseases that will further inform our understanding of RYTELO's clinical potential. Our 6 accepted abstracts at ASH reinforce the clinical and biological evidence of RYTELO and we look forward to sharing additional details later today. Our progress has been recognized beyond the medical community. We are honored to have been nominated for the Prix Galien USA Award for Best Product for Orphan or Rare Diseases.

This recognition represents decades of pioneering work in telomerase inhibition and most importantly, a sustained commitment to addressing significant unmet need for people living with low-risk MDS. It is a meaningful acknowledgment of the science behind RYTELO and the potential to translate that science into better outcomes for patients. I'll now hand it over to Michelle to walk through the financials.

Michelle Robertson: Thank you, Joe, and good morning, everyone. For more detailed results from the third quarter, please refer to the press release we issued this morning, which is available on our website. Our third quarter financial results highlight the progress we are making on our commercial strategy and operational excellence. We are in a strong financial position with a balance sheet that enables targeted and disciplined investments into further growth opportunities, including business development. In the third quarter, total net product revenue for the 3 months ended September 30, 2026, was $60.1 million compared to $47.2 million in Q3 of 2025.

Gross to net deductions decreased to 19.3% for the 3 months ended September 30, 2026 compared to 21.6% for the same period in 2025. For the remainder of 2026, we continue to expect gross to net to be in the low to mid-20s. Research and development expenses for the 3 months ended September 30, 2026, were $12.7 million compared to $21.1 million in expenses for the same period in 2025. The decrease in research and development expenses was a result of lower headcount costs from the workforce reduction in December 2025 and lower clinical chemistry manufacturing and control costs. For the remainder of 2026, we expect continued investment in CMC and our clinical post-marketing commitments, offset by lower employee costs.

Due to wind-down activities, we do not expect any significant decrease in spending on our MF program in 2026. Selling, general and administrative expenses for the 3 months ended September 30, 2026, were $35.7 million compared to $39 million for the same period in 2025. This decrease was primarily due to lower general and administrative personnel-related expenses as a result of the workforce reduction in December 2025. Total operating expenses, excluding COGS, for the 3 months ended September 30, 2026 were $48.3 million compared to $60.1 million for the same period in 2025.

As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately $339 million in cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and marketable securities compared to $327 million as of June 30, 2026. We are committed to maintaining our financial discipline and are well positioned to fund growth from our current operations. We are reiterating our 2026 RYTELO net revenue guidance with the expectation we will come in at the mid- to high end of the $220 million to $240 million range, reflecting consistent quarter-over-quarter net revenue growth throughout the year. We are lowering our total operating expense guidance from $230 million to $240 million to the range of $220 million to $230 million.

This reduction reflects our ability to drive continued operational excellence, while also making strategic investments into RYTELO and future growth opportunities. With $339 million in cash, we are well positioned to execute on our financial and strategic priorities through the remainder of the year. With that, I'll turn the call back to Harout for closing remarks.

Harout Semerjian: Thanks, Michelle. RYTELO has grown for 4 consecutive quarters, placing us on track to achieve our 2026 net revenue guidance and maximize our long-term growth potential. Beyond RYTELO, our financial strength gives us the flexibility to explore business development opportunities to build a leading hematology company. Operator, we're now ready to start the Q&A session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question comes from Tara Bancroft of TD Cowen.

Tara Bancroft: So it's great to see the reduced OpEx guidance this year. It all makes sense. But I'm wondering how we should think about OpEx expectations really going forward, especially with the MF Phase III not factored in. If there are any savings from that? Harout Semerjian: Yes. Thank you, Tara. Maybe that's a question Michelle can address.

Michelle Robertson: Yes. Thanks, Tara. So yes, we reduced our OpEx for 2026. What I would say about the go-forward investments, we'll continue to be very disciplined in our capital allocation. Gil Blum: Congrats on the progress here. So definitely seeing consistent growth quarter-over-quarter kind of in the low -- in the single digits. What do you think could cause a rate change or change in the rate of uptake that would be more of an acceleration? And is this something we should expect? Or should we continue to see this kind of like consistent growth over time? And I have a follow-up.

Harout Semerjian: Thank you, Gil. As we have communicated multiple quarters ago, the way we look at RYTELO's growth, if we do things well, is it will deliver consistent growth quarter-over-quarter, and we're very pleased today to announce the fourth quarter of that strategy in action where we continue every quarter to increase demand to increase sales, to increase penetration in the first-line, second-line market patient segment and to reduce OpEx. And we do believe that there are thousands of more patients who can benefit from RYTELO for many years to come. That's why we do see the long-term perspective of RYTELO growth are quite good. But can you maybe speak to any differences in how the disease might be managed there just relative to the U.S.? I guess when I look at REBLOZYL, they're generating, I think, less than 20% of their sales ex U.S., which I'm sure is partially pricing-based, but would perhaps suggest some differences in terms of how the disease is managed.

Harout Semerjian: Sure. Maybe I'll start off and then ElNawawi can supplement as well. Look, I mean, from a patient perspective, it's really the same size of number of patients that we have in the U.S., in the U.S. we have said about 8,000 patients would be eligible for that second line patient population. And then as you know, European, average age is even older, so it's at least that number of patients from a macro perspective overall. The reason obviously, we're choosing Germany to go with. I mean that is the country where you have a meaningful path for innovation in a healthy pricing point in line with the innovation that we can bring.

ElNawawi, do you want to add on top of that additional reasons to believe?

Ahmed ElNawawi: Sure. And a couple of points maybe Steve, you referred to REBLOZYL, they have gone through several price iterations because of their broader label and multiple indications. We are a single indication drug with an orphan designation, which does give us high scoring, especially in Germany reimbursement perspective, plus the market is not as diversified in terms of payment options in Europe compared to the U.S., where in the U.S., we see a much higher use of HMA in second and third line, which is not reflect what the European market, so we see a bit of differences and [ by vote ].

Harout Semerjian: Yes. And just to be -- also address, the REBLOZYL point you made, Steve. I mean that is you -- probably know that, that in most European markets, it is restricted to Rh positive. And I mean, typically larger pharma has to think about the portfolio overall, especially protecting larger products like their PD-1s. We don't have that hindrance in that way, so we have a label that we can pursue especially in a Rh negative patient population, orphan designation. HMAs are not as entrenched in Europe, older population. And as you know, the clinical trial we had, IMerge, was predominantly European. So there's significant advocacy as well from the medical community wanting to see RYTELO available for that patient.

Stephen Willey: Congratulations on achieving profitability.

Operator: Thank you. I show no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn it back to Harout Semerjian for closing remarks.

Harout Semerjian: Thank you to everyone joining our call today. We look forward to updating you on the progress in the next several quarters. Thank you.

Both the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard®  and Citi Strata Premier® Card can help you rack up AAdvantage miles. The former earns them directly; the latter transfers points to American Airlines at a 1:1 ratio. So which one is better for American Airlines flyers?

For earning rewards, the Citi Strata Premier® Card is the winner. Although it's not an American Airlines credit card, it can make it easier to accumulate AAdvantage miles on many purchases with its higher earning rates and the option to transfer ThankYou points to American.

Still, the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® can help you achieve AAdvantage elite status and offers perks when flying American Airlines, including a free checked bag and preferred boarding. In 2027, the annual fee will increase, but the card will add new bonus categories and other benefits.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card is a better fit for travelers who want to earn American Airlines miles without committing all their rewards to a single airline program.

Although the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® is an American Airlines credit card, the Citi Strata Premier® Card can be a faster way to accumulate AAdvantage miles on many purchases.

That's because Citi Strata Premier® Card holders can transfer ThankYou points to American Airlines AAdvantage — and several other loyalty programs — at a 1:1 ratio.

Currently, the Citi Strata Premier® Card offers more rewards than the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® in every bonus category. On Jan. 24, 2027, when the benefits on the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® change, that will change — but only in a couple of narrowly defined categories: select streaming services and eligible Rides and Rails purchases, which include taxis, rideshares, subways and trains. Unless those categories make up a significant portion of your spending, the Citi Strata Premier® Card will likely yield more points overall, even if your ultimate goal is American Airlines miles.

» Learn more: 11 Benefits of the Citi Strata Premier® Card

The Citi Strata Premier® Card also offers a $100 annual hotel benefit when you book a single hotel stay of $500 or more, excluding taxes and fees, through Citi Travel. Using the full benefit can more than offset the card’s annual fee, and hotel bookings through Citi Travel earn 10 ThankYou points per dollar.

Just keep in mind that booking through Citi Travel may mean giving up hotel loyalty program benefits you would receive by booking directly. Whether the $100 hotel perk offers enough value to justify booking through Citi Travel will depend on the property, the rates available and how much you value those hotel loyalty benefits.

» Learn more: Is the Citi Strata Premier® Card worth its annual fee?

One of the biggest advantages of the Citi Strata Premier® Card is the ability to earn ThankYou points, which can be transferred to several airline and hotel loyalty programs. If you want the option to transfer points to American Airlines but also see value in the card’s other airline and hotel partners, the Citi Strata Premier® Card is a better choice.
