Free checked bag: Get a free first checked bag on domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardholder and up to four companions traveling on the same reservation. If you check bags with American, this benefit alone could make the card worth getting.

Preferred boarding: The primary cardholder and up to four companions on the same reservation receive preferred boarding.

The inflight statement credits, in particular, will be easy to maximize and could potentially offset a meaningful portion of the card’s annual fee. Combined with the ability to earn Loyalty Points toward elite status and the card’s other perks, that can make the card more valuable for American’s flyers.

It’s unusual to see a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit on a card with an annual fee under $200. Cardholders receive 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile earned from purchases. That means everyday spending can move you closer to AAdvantage elite status, in addition to earning miles you can redeem for flights. If you want to earn rewards on everyday spending and have the flexibility to move those points to American Airlines — and you don’t need the airline-specific benefits — the Citi Strata Premier® Card is the best choice.

That said, the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® makes more sense for frequent American Airlines flyers who can take advantage of benefits such as a free checked bag and preferred boarding, or for travelers who want to earn Loyalty Points toward American Airlines elite status through credit card spending.

#3062. Coupang vs. Five Below: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy Going Into 2027?

Coupang's cash-rich Korean delivery empire goes head-to-head with Five Below's teen-focused bargain stores, but their valuations tell very different stories.

Investors looking for growth often weigh domestic value against international scale. Choosing between Coupang (CPNG +11.95%) and Five Below (FIVE +6.70%) requires balancing South Korea's e-commerce dominance against a rapidly expanding U.S. discount retailer.

Coupang operates a massive logistics network to deliver everything from groceries to electronics across South Korea and Taiwan. Five Below focuses on high-energy, low-cost treasure hunts for American youth. Both companies aim to capture market share in the evolving retail landscape, though their geographic footprints and operational models offer distinct paths for long-term growth.

Coupang provides retail, restaurant delivery, and video streaming services through brands like Rocket Now and the WOW membership program. The company serves millions of active customers in South Korea and Taiwan, leveraging its own logistics infrastructure to ensure rapid delivery. Its strategic partnership with Sartori Cheese highlights its focus on distributing perishable U.S. goods to international markets.

In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $34.5 billion, marking an increase of approximately 14.1% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net income of $208.0 million for the period. This growth follows a steady upward trajectory in sales despite fluctuating net margin levels in previous fiscal cycles.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.0x, meaning its total debt is equal to its shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with current assets, was 1.0x. For FY 2025, free cash flow reached $522.0 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 26.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Five Below operates a value-based retail model targeting kids, teens, and pre-teens with trend-right merchandise. The company manages over 2,000 stores across the U.S., offering products in categories like tech, sports, and fashion. It works with roughly 1,000 vendors to maintain its diverse inventory without relying too heavily on any single supplier.

In FY 2025, revenue reached $4.8 billion, representing growth of 22.9% over the previous fiscal year. Net income for the period was $358.6 million, with a net margin of 7.5%. This performance reflects the company's ability to drive sales through both new store openings and existing locations, a key strength among retail stocks.

Based on its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.9x, indicating total debt is slightly lower than shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at 2.0x, indicating a strong capacity to cover near-term liabilities with liquid assets. In FY 2025, the company generated free cash flow of $411.7 million, providing capital for further store expansion.

Five Below is exposed to inflation and rising product costs, which can impact its low-price value proposition. The company depends on merchandise manufactured outside the U.S., making it sensitive to tariffs and trade volatility. Furthermore, it faces legal risks from class action lawsuits regarding growth and inventory management misstatements that could impact future results.

Five Below appears cheaper based on future earnings estimates, while Coupang offers a lower P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Between retail players Coupang and Five Below, I would buy Five Below. Coupang's e-commerce business relies heavily on its South Korean customers, yet the company suffered a black eye when it was hacked last year, prompting investigations by the Korean government.

In addition, since the incident was revealed in November of 2025, Coupang's sales growth has steadily declined. Before the data breach was revealed, the company's revenue in the third quarter of 2025 grew 18% year over year. That dropped to 11% in Q4 after the incident was publicized. Sales continued falling in 2026, and in Q2, year-over-year sales growth had slowed to 4%.

Coupang saw some recovery in Q3 of this year, as revenue rose 7% year over year to $10 billion. Even so, investors should monitor the situation to see if the company continues to gain steam in subsequent quarters.

Meanwhile, Five Below is enjoying robust growth in 2026 despite the volatile macroeconomic background. In its fiscal Q2, ended Aug. 1, sales grew 23% to $1.3 billion. The company also raised its 2026 full-year revenue outlook to a range between $5.6 billion to $5.7 billion, up from 2025's $4.8 billion. Five Below's business is doing well and shows no signs of slowing down.

#3060. A massive trade just happened in surging shares of Snap

Don't call it a comeback yet, but shares of beleaguered social media stock Snap Inc. are up almost 20% this month and options traders are betting it's about to go on a big run.Snap shares have traded under $10 since July 2025 following a near-complete collapse from over $80 at the stock's high in 2021 to a low of $3.81 in April. But now, as excitement swirls over social media giant Meta Platforms' AI agent, traders are pouring into Snap call options on Monday, propelling trading volume to more than four times the month-long average, Cboe LiveVol data show.Almost 140,000 options on Snap traded Monday, including about 64,000 call trades that were likely initiated by buyers, compared to under 7,000 puts. Traders sold more than 12,000 puts, and just over 34,000 calls. The net trade sentiment, as well as net directional bias according to options deltas, was positive, according to Barchart.

Nine out of the top 10 trades by volume were calls, and of the $5.5 million in premium exchanged, $5 million was tied to calls, SpotGamma data show.The most popular contract to buy was the 8-strike call expiring Dec. 18, which traded 26,000 times. That contract costs about 37 cents and needs Snap to rally 30% before expiry to pay off. If that happens, it would be the highest the stock's traded since February.The owner of photo-sharing and messaging app Snapchat also offers augmented-reality `Specs' glasses. Shareholder Blue Duck Capital issued an open letter to Snap's board of directors last week urging the company to raise dedicated capital to support the product, saying it could lead to a $12-$14 share price.

#3059. Management Mistakes That Throttle Innovation On Tech Teams

Tech leaders often say they want their teams to experiment and pursue new ideas. But even seemingly reasonable management practices can make creative risks feel too costly or time-consuming. When those pressures become part of everyday work, employees may become less willing to test unfamiliar approaches or challenge established ways of working.

The disconnect between encouraging innovation and making room for it isn’t always obvious to leaders. Here, members of Forbes Technology Council explore the management habits that can quietly hold innovation back and explain what leaders can do differently to support experimentation.

The mistake is making every experiment a delivery commitment. Having managed program managers and engineers, I’d separate learning goals from ship dates. Only 13% of AI users in Microsoft’s 2026 survey said reinvention was rewarded when results fell short. Set a question, a budget and a stop date; disproving the idea can still be a useful result. - Swapnil Upganlawar, Amazon

Blanket bans and strict restrictions on AI tools kill innovation. Blocking doesn’t stop adoption. It creates an AI lockdown paradox, where employees move their work to personal devices and accounts. Leaders end up with all of the security risk and none of the visibility. Instead of acting as the “Department of No,” leaders should put automated guardrails in place that let teams experiment safely. - Rick Caccia, WitnessAI

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Only rewarding safe goals undermines innovation. If people are judged only on goals, they make conservative plans and stop proposing big bets. We want people who set goals they might miss and run their area like owners. We judge them on how far they moved the business and what they learned. - Chris Szymansky, Fieldguide

Rushing teams into execution before giving them space to understand, experiment and learn stifles experimentation. Innovation suffers when leaders don’t take the time to deeply understand the problem, connect it to a meaningful business outcome, and bring the right cross-functional teams together. Release in small, meaningful increments; test, learn and iterate. Great innovation needs both freedom to experiment and discipline around outcomes. - Benu Aggarwal, Milestone, Inc.

Punishing failed experiments while celebrating innovation holds teams back. When leaders demand certainty before approving new ideas or judge every experiment by immediate returns, teams learn that playing it safe is rewarded. Innovation requires disciplined experimentation, clear boundaries and permission to learn. The real test of leadership is not how it celebrates success but how it responds when a well-designed experiment fails. - Maman Ibrahim, EugeneZonda

Overengineering experimentation quietly kills innovation. Discipline matters, but every experiment doesn’t need to become a project. Give teams a clear problem, guardrails and the autonomy to test, learn and iterate quickly. The goal isn’t less process. It’s making sure the process serves innovation—not the other way around. - Abhijit Kakhandiki, BMC Software

Filling every sprint to 100% quietly kills innovation. Leaders say they want experiments, then plan the roadmap so tightly that there is no room to try anything. People will not test a new idea when it means missing a committed deadline. If experimentation matters, it needs space on the calendar. Keep some capacity unplanned and protect it when delivery pressure builds. - Mudit Singh, TestMu AI (LambdaTest)

Starting with features instead of user problems kills innovation. When epics and features are defined before the team understands user needs, experimentation is compressed into implementation. UX and delivery teams are left optimizing a predetermined solution instead of using discovery to jointly design a better one. Engage UX strategists from the start. This gives teams the greatest autonomy to design the best solution. - April Ho-Nishimura, Infineon Technologies AG

Prioritizing trends and buzzwords over how comfortable employees are with adopting new technologies can undermine innovation. Leaders may see a new tool or tech stack as an opportunity to innovate, but forcing it on a team without considering their experience can have the opposite effect. Innovation works best when people have the time, support and freedom to explore technology rather than simply follow trends. - Artem Lalaiants, RiskSeal, Inc.

Treating the existing workflow as untouchable quietly kills innovation. In recent banking discussions, leaders emphasized redesigning the process before deciding where AI belongs. Asking teams to experiment while preserving every approval, handoff and metric limits what they can discover. Give teams permission to question how work gets done and test a better way with clear guardrails and outcomes. - Gregg Aldana, Appian

Demanding outcomes without fostering the culture that supports innovation is counterproductive. Leadership needs to put more emphasis on people as half of the factors in successful outcomes. Providing your people with a culture that fosters creativity, open debate and collaboration is necessary for experimentation and for turning that experimentation into commercial products. - Susan Odle, StorMagic

Giving teams a destination when what they need is a direction limits innovation. A list of approved projects only contains what leadership has imagined, so teams never get past those ideas. With AI, we set clear limits on data access, then handed every department a blank page and one direction: Try things and find your own use cases. Ideas came from every function, not from the plan we drew up in advance. - Alex Saric, Ivalua

Requiring a business case before anyone is allowed to try something can shut down experimentation. Leaders say they want experimentation, then ask for projected ROI on a two-week test, which guarantees that only safe, incremental ideas get proposed. Give teams a small preapproved budget and time box for experiments, and ask for a business case only after the test produces evidence. - Agung Dwi Sandi, rankpillar Group

Judging experiments by the same metrics as established products quietly kills innovation. Teams learn to protect quarterly targets instead of testing bold ideas. A space mission needs ground tests that expose weaknesses before launch; tech teams need that same permission to discover what fails. The space mindset: Reward disciplined learning, with clear hypotheses, bounded resources and evidence that informs the next decision. Make learning a performance goal. - Shelli Brunswick, SB Global LLC

Roadmaps and dates can constrain innovation. Often, management is trying to forecast the impact of things on the business, and because of this, they put expectations around dates, delivery and impact. But innovation requires a lot of experimentation, and the first version is often not correct or impactful in the way you expect. It is the constant iteration that drives real results, and that is hard to quantify and predict. - Mark Beare, Malwarebytes

Having to report to a CFO to justify market demand when the technology has not even been prototyped, tested or taken to market is a sure way to kill innovation. While innovation teams need to work in a resource-disciplined manner, finance should not have a seat at the table during the early stages of innovation, concepting and user testing. - Mark Francis, CaregiverZone

Innovation must not be limited by a long list of constraints. It also must be presented to the right audience. Wheeled luggage was patented in 1970 but did not become widely popular until two decades later. How management delivers their message when an innovative idea presented does not meet current needs is critical. For example, “That’s not what I am looking for” versus “How do you see this idea resolving the issues in front of us?” create two different impacts. - Irene Thong, Oglethorpe Power

Requiring too many layers of approval before anyone can test an idea discourages innovation. Having worked through several major technology shifts, I’ve learned that you rarely know exactly what will work until you try it. When every experiment requires multiple meetings and executive sign-off, people stop bringing forward ideas. Give teams room to test things without making them defend every idea first. - Nada Usina, NU Advisory Partners

Rewarding people for knowing rather than learning stifles innovation. When teams are expected to have the right answer before they experiment, they stick to familiar problems and safer solutions. Leaders need to make it easier to be wrong, test assumptions and learn quickly. The point of experimentation isn’t always to succeed. Sometimes it’s simply to find out what doesn’t work and why. - Dhiraj Rajaram, Mu Sigma

Mortgage rates jumped after stronger-than-expected jobs data raised expectations for a Fed rate hike next month.

Mortgage rates are higher today on the heels of strong labor market data released yesterday.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points higher than yesterday but 25 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

Mortgage rates are always on the move, so if you're tracking rates day-to-day, you're going to see a lot of volatility.

As for today’s jump: Job openings hit a four-month high of 7.5 million in September, according to the Labor Department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey released yesterday. Hiring picked up, too, while layoffs declined. Friday’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.57% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

» Get the best rate for you: How to get the best mortgage rate

Maybe — but even personalized rate quotes can change until you lock. That’s because lenders adjust pricing multiple times a day in response to market changes.

#3056. Celsius vs. Chipotle Mexican Grill: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Celsius trades at a cheaper valuation but depends heavily on Pepsi for distribution, while Chipotle comes with its own set of risks.

Investors often weigh the hyper-growth of beverage upstarts against the steady expansion of established restaurant chains. Choosing between Celsius (CELH +2.57%) and Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG +5.83%) requires balancing immediate revenue surges with long-term stability.

Celsius focuses on functional energy drinks that appeal to health-conscious consumers, while Chipotle dominates the fast-casual dining space with its fresh-ingredient philosophy. Both companies rely on strong brand loyalty to navigate competitive retail environments. We will examine their financial health and market risks to determine which aligns better with your 2027 investing goals.

Celsius sells functional beverages through major retailers, fitness centers, and e-commerce platforms. Its growth strategy relies heavily on a partnership with Pepsi, which serves as its primary U.S. distributor and helps manage brands like Rockstar. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, which is something to keep in mind.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $2.5 billion, representing growth of approximately 85.5% over the previous year. This rapid expansion helped the company achieve net income of roughly $108 million.

Chipotle Mexican Grill operates a massive network of company-owned restaurants, focusing on a "food with integrity" mission. According to its latest annual report, filed for the period ending December 31, 2025, the company owned over 4,000 locations globally. It reaches customers through physical stores and digital channels, including platforms owned by Amazon (AMZN +6.12%).

In FY 2025, revenue reached $11.9 billion, a growth of roughly 5.4% compared to the prior fiscal year. Net income for the period was nearly $1.5 billion, resulting in a healthy net margin of approximately 12.9%. This consistent profitability highlights the company's ability to manage costs effectively across its large-scale restaurant operations.

Celsius faces significant revenue concentration with Pepsi, creating a heavy reliance on a single distribution partner for its core business. The company also deals with operational risks from third-party co-packers and intense competition from Monster Beverage (MNST +3.33%). Rapid growth could also lead to brand cannibalization as it integrates acquired businesses or expands its product lines.

Chipotle Mexican Grill is vulnerable to food safety risks that could damage its brand reputation due to its reliance on fresh, unprocessed ingredients. It relies heavily on third-party delivery services and faces pressure from large competitors like McDonald's (MCD +6.53%). Rising labor costs and potential supply chain disruptions also present ongoing challenges for its business model.

Celsius appears more attractively priced based on traditional metrics.

This is an interesting stock battle, as each company could fit into a portfolio to serve different purposes. With Celsius, you're looking at more of a growth stock. It's carving out a niche in the energy drink market, which is expected to be a global industry valued at $157.2 billion, according to Fortune Business Insights. Celsius can continue to capture that growing revenue opportunity by having more products on the shelves, as it acquired the energy drink maker Alani Nutrition in 2025.

Chipotle, on the other hand, is a more mature company, but that comes with its own set of benefits. As we saw earlier, Chipotle generates more revenue than Celsius, hauling in $11.9 billion in fiscal 2025 compared to Celsius's $2.5 billion. It's also capturing more profits, with Chipotle's net income over that period totaling $1.5 billion while Celsius reported $108 million in net income.

Between the two, heading into 2027, I would rather own shares of Chipotle. With plenty of uncertainty still swirling around the markets, Chipotle offers more stability as a more established business, but it also still has revenue growth opportunities. The restaurant chain has a long-term goal of operating 7,000 locations in North America, so that can help sales keep climbing. And while Celsius may have more stock price growth potential ahead, that also comes with greater risk. For example, over the last 12 months, shares of Chipotle are up 9.4%, while shares of Celsius are down nearly 48%. While both are underperforming the S&P 500's 13.6% return over that period, Chipotle's positive returns indicate greater stability than Celsius, a high-risk, high-reward stock.

#3052. Mine, Enrich, Build, Operate: Which Link in the Nuclear Supply Chain Is the Best Stock Right Now?

With demand for electricity growing at a rapid clip, nuclear power is increasingly important.

Oklo (OKLO -5.83%) is looking to build a business around small modular nuclear reactors, putting it at the forefront of the nuclear power industry. NextEra Energy (NEE +4.89%) sells power from nuclear power plants it owns, with its proposed acquisition of Dominion (D +4.45%) set to make it the number two player in nuclear power in the United States. And then there are intermediaries, like fuel supplier Cameco (CCJ -1.21%) or service provider Westinghouse, which is owned by Cameco and Brookfield Renewable Partners (BEP +2.01%).

For most investors, keeping your nuclear power exposure simple and diversified is probably the best choice. And that suggests that NextEra Energy or a competitor like Constellation Energy (CEG -6.71%), the largest U.S. nuclear operator, could be the best option. Here's why.

Oklo is a money-losing start-up with new nuclear technology. Only the most aggressive investors should even consider it. Cameco's business is heavily driven by uranium prices, which can be highly volatile. While its Westinghouse investment should help to provide more reliable revenues, that's just one part of the business. Meanwhile, Brookfield Renewable Partners is really a much broader bet on clean energy. Westinghouse, which it partially owns with Cameco, is a relatively small part of the business.

Meanwhile, NextEra and Constellation are both heavily invested in nuclear power to support the growth in electricity demand. They are more direct plays on the space in some ways, while also offering a more conservative profile. NextEra is a regulated utility, while Constellation sells power under long-term contracts. Both are set to benefit as electricity demand, including demand for their large nuclear operations, is projected to grow 60% between 2025 and 2045, up from just 10% in the prior 20-year period.

That said, Constellation and NextEra are very different businesses. NextEra offers a well-above-market 2.9% yield backed by 31 annual dividend increases. It's probably the best choice for more conservative income investors looking to add nuclear exposure to their portfolios. Constellation's yield is just 0.6%, while selling power at market rates would allow it to benefit more from demand-led price increases. It's more appropriate for growth investors.

While Oklo or Cameco would be more exciting and more closely tied to nuclear's future, they also involve much more risk. Brookfield Renewable also sells power under long-term contracts, but it is really a highly focused play on clean energy. Nuclear giants NextEra and Constellation probably offer the best balance of risk and reward, with the option to lean toward income or growth depending on your preference.

#3051. Pet Insurance on Your Mind? Buy It Now, Not Later

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

If your pet is young and healthy, the cost of coverage may not seem worth it. But that math can change fast.

Senior Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3043. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3031. Better Nuclear Energy Stock to Buy After the Sell-Off: Oklo vs. BWX Technologies

Nuclear stocks are in a sell-off, and there might be opportunities for investors at these prices.

Electricity demand is rising due to artificial intelligence (AI), and nuclear energy is set to meet it. At least, if you look at the charts of nuclear power stocks last year, that's what you would assume was the case. Now, not so much.

Nuclear power stocks have faltered in 2026, even though the AI infrastructure build-out continues. Oklo (OKLO -5.83%) is down 86% from highs, while BWX Technologies (BWXT -7.83%) is down 45%. Is either nuclear energy-related stock a buy after this sell-off? It is clear when you look closer at the numbers.

You may have never heard of BWX Technologies, but it has been a mainstay in the nuclear energy field for decades. It builds nuclear reactors for the U.S. Navy, powering aircraft carriers and submarines. These contracts have long lead times and span multiple decades, meaning BWX Technologies can generate reliable revenue from them for many years. It is also working on futuristic nuclear power technologies for the U.S., including space-based nuclear propulsion and microreactors.

On the commercial side, BWX has a durable business selling components to the nuclear power market in Canada and is trying to sell more components for small modular reactors (SMRs), already having contracts with GE Hitachi and other players, although it is still very early days for the segment. Commercial revenue grew 25% year over year to $314 million.

Overall, revenue grew 10% year over year in the third quarter to $953 million. It is expected to generate around $350 million in free cash flow this year, implying a price-to-free cash flow (P/FCF) ratio of 34x based on its current market cap. Next year, free cash flow is expected to be at a similar level, which is perhaps why BWX Technologies is down this year, but the long-term growth trajectory for its place in the nuclear power sector is rock solid.

Speaking of SMRs, Oklo is a start-up trying to bring this technology to life. The company has raised billions of dollars to build a modern SMR business for power, fuel, and isotopes. It wants to have nuclear reactor facilities directly built for AI data centers.

Oklo does not have any reactors built today. In fact, it does not have a nuclear reactor design officially approved by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). Without NRC approval, it will not be able to build actual nuclear reactors.

This puts the business many years away from full operations. It is working to produce nuclear fuel and isotopes, which may add some revenue to the business, but the core thesis centers on Oklo's Aurora Powerhouse nuclear reactor, which it hopes to sell by the boatload in the years ahead to power AI data centers and other electricity needs in the United States.

Right now, Oklo's revenue is basically zero. It will likely stay there for many years. Even if it gets approval from the NRC tomorrow, it will take years before a nuclear reactor is actually built and operational.

Oklo's stock has crashed this year, much more than BWX Technologies'. It has a market cap of $4.3 billion, compared with $12 billion for BWX Technologies.

Even though Oklo is now at a much lower price, BWX Technologies looks like a better buy because of its diversified bets across the nuclear supply chain. The military contracts will remain steady, and its forays into new commercial opportunities are potentially promising if SMRs truly are the future of the sector.

For this reason -- along with the lack of revenue generation at Oklo -- BWX Technologies is a better stock to buy on the nuclear energy sell-off.

#3023. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3022. AMD Stock Jumped After Its Report. I'd Wait for a Lower Price to Buy.

The chipmaker now expects its revenue to rise over 80% next year. What's a fair price to pay for that?

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +1.01%) gave investors a big number on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Along with its third-quarter results, management said on the earnings call that it now expects revenue to rise over 80% in 2027. That's more than double the annual growth in the long-term model AMD set out at its financial analyst day last November.

Shares jumped. After closing Tuesday at $483.90, the stock gained about 7.5% in after-hours trading to roughly $520. The stock has given back most of that gain since, and at around $490 as I write, it's about 25% under $649.42, the record close on Oct. 6.

On Oct. 27, I wrote that I'd hold a small position in AMD through 2030, though I wouldn't expect the stock to triple again. The report doesn't change that long view. What it does change is how much weight I'd give next year's earnings -- enough to set a price on them.

Showing how fast the company is scaling, AMD's third-quarter revenue climbed 45% year over year to $13.4 billion, and non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share jumped 74% to $2.09.

The data center segment, which sells server processors and artificial intelligence (AI) chips, powered most of that growth. Its revenue almost doubled, climbing 97% from a year ago to a record $8.5 billion, up from $6.7 billion in the second quarter and $5.8 billion in the first. Notably, its quarter-to-quarter growth picked up from 16% in the second quarter to 27% in the latest one. And the segment now makes up 64% of AMD's revenue, up from 47% a year ago.

The fourth-quarter forecast is even steeper.

AMD expects around $17 billion in revenue, up about 66% from a year earlier and 27% from the third quarter. Management expects growth to speed up as AMD scales production of Helios, its rack-scale AI system.

Earnings are soaring, but the cash isn't keeping up. AMD's free cash flow dropped to $554 million in the third quarter, or around 4% of revenue, down from $1.5 billion in the year-ago quarter. And it has fallen in both of the past two quarters, from around $2.6 billion in the first quarter to $1.6 billion in the second.

Most of the gap between profit and cash went to inventory. AMD's stockpile grew around $3 billion from June to September, to $11.5 billion, bringing this year's build to about $3.5 billion. Capital spending is climbing, too. AMD spent around $650 million on property and equipment in the third quarter, up from about $260 million a year ago.

And management expects to keep spending on both.

"We expect to continue to invest in inventory and capacity to support our strong growth in 2027," CFO Jean Hu said on the call.

Put simply, AMD is paying up front for next year's sales. Yes, that's arguably the right move for a company whose CEO, Lisa Su, said demand is outpacing supply. But it also means earnings come in well before cash does.

Of course, if customers put off their deployments, $11.5 billion of inventory might become a problem.

On average, analysts expect AMD's adjusted earnings per share to hit about $16 in 2027. That's around double the $8 or so it looks on track to earn this year: $5.12 through September, plus about $2.90 implied by its fourth-quarter guidance for revenue, margins, spending, tax and share count.

Management's forecast makes the 2027 estimate look reachable. Besides the revenue growth of over 80%, Hu said AMD expects operating expenses next year to rise at under half that pace, which could lift its profit margin.

At around $490, the stock has a price-to-earnings ratio of about 31 on AMD's expected 2027 earnings. For comparison, the forward price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%), based on the next 12 months of expected earnings, is about 19. AMD can justify a hefty premium to that if its earnings double as expected. Still, I don't want to pay much more than around 30 times expected 2027 earnings, mostly because of the cash.

At 30 times earnings, my buy price is about $480. That's near Tuesday's close and a little below where the stock trades now.

Overall, the report made me more confident about AMD's 2027 outlook. But the company still needs to convert those earnings into cash, and the stock already prices in much of that growth.

At or below $480, I think AMD stock is worth considering for a small position. At roughly $490, I'd wait.

Intuitive Machines vs. Rocket Lab Revenue over the last 8 quarters.

#3015. IonQ vs. SoundHound AI: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

IonQ trades at a premium, while SoundHound AI shows a clearer path to profitability.

Emerging technology sectors offer high growth potential but often carry significant risks for early investors. Let's explore whether IonQ (IONQ -1.50%) or SoundHound AI (SOUN +4.85%) is the better long-term choice for your portfolio.

IonQ is a leader in quantum computing, a field that uses subatomic physics to perform calculations beyond the reach of traditional computers. SoundHound AI specializes in conversational voice technology for various consumer and commercial applications. Both companies are in their early expansion phases and represent different ways to play the broader artificial intelligence (AI) trend.

IonQ specializes in trapped-ion quantum computing, selling hardware access and networking solutions to a variety of commercial and government clients. Its technology is available through major cloud platforms like Amazon (AMZN +6.12%), Microsoft (MSFT +6.68%), and the marketplace for Alphabet. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. The company also operates within the broader semiconductor stocks category by developing specialized hardware for quantum sensing and positioning applications.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $130 million, representing a significant increase of approximately 201.9% compared to the previous year. Despite this rapid growth, the company reported a net loss of close to $510.4 million for the period. The company is still spending heavily to develop its technology and scale its workforce.

SoundHound AI provides conversational voice software that powers digital assistants in cars, restaurants, and consumer devices. The company expanded its reach in the technology sector by acquiring LivePerson in 2026. This move helps the firm offer a more comprehensive platform for customer service and automated voice interactions. Its strategy focuses on building long-term partnerships with original equipment manufacturers and hospitality brands to secure recurring revenue streams.

In FY 2025, revenue reached close to $168.9 million, which is an increase of approximately 99.4% over the prior year. The company reported a net loss of nearly $14 million for the fiscal period. Its net margin improved significantly year over year, reaching roughly negative 8.3%, suggesting the business is moving closer toward breaking even more than some of its peers in the emerging tech space.

IonQ faces significant risks as an early-stage company with a history of operating losses and no track record of large-scale commercial production. Key risks include intense global competition from well established technology companies and the unproven nature of its business model. The company also faces potential delays in technical roadmaps and high revenue concentration among a small number of customers.

SoundHound AI is subject to risks related to its substantial operating losses and negative cash flows as it continues to scale its operations. The company has identified material weaknesses in its internal control over financial reporting, which could impact the accuracy of its financial disclosures. It faces competition from massive technology firms and relies on a few key customers and original equipment manufacturing partners. Integration challenges following acquisitions such as LivePerson and Amelia also create operational and legal risks as the company deploys generative AI solutions.

SoundHound AI offers a lower price-to-sales (P/S) ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months, compared to the much higher premium assigned to IonQ.

This is a tough battle because you have two high-growth stocks that are part of two massive investing trends: quantum computing and AI. For quantum computing, IonQ is considered one of the few pure-play options out there, and if you're going to own any quantum stock, it's high on the list of options to consider. Ultimately, I can see both fitting into a portfolio as small, speculative positions. But if just one stock is going to be picked between the two, I would go with SoundHound.

The simple reason is that quantum computing is still just in its very early stages. According to Fortune Business Insights, the global quantum computing market was valued at $1.3 billion in 2025 and is expected to climb to $17.8 billion by 2034. There's solid growth there, but it's just not as large as the AI industry. In comparison, according to Statista, the global AI market is forecast to reach $1.9 trillion by 2032.

SoundHound also has an advantage in that it currently offers more mainstream use cases for its technology, with clients like Five Guys and Panda Express, financial services companies, automakers, and more. We'll soon see more updates on how the company has recently fared, as it is expected to report earnings on Nov. 5. Still, even if those results aren't favorable, between the two, for the foreseeable future, I would rather own SoundHound because the quantum market may take longer to develop and have less market value than AI for some time.

#3014. SpaceX Just Picked Qualcomm for Its Own 5G Network. I Still See the Stock as a Hold.

Tens of thousands of cell sites start going up in 2027. How much of that belongs in the stock price now?

SpaceX (SPCX -3.81%) now has a supplier for the ground side of its plan to become a U.S. wireless carrier. Qualcomm (QCOM +5.33%) said on Wednesday that SpaceX chose its Dragonwing cellular infrastructure platforms for Starlink Mobile's nationwide ground-based 5G network. SpaceX plans to start the rollout in 2027, with tens of thousands of sites deployed over the multiyear agreement. Neither company shared financial terms.

SpaceX stock slid anyway. Shares traded near $136 as I write, off about 3% on the day and almost a third under their record close of $201.80.

Does the deal turn Starlink Mobile into a true rival to the big carriers? I think it pushes the plan forward, but I doubt it changes much for the stock yet.

Qualcomm is providing two platforms, its QRU100 for the radio units and its QDU100 for processing signals, plus the Layer 1 software that runs the network's physical radio layer. The radios will use 64 transmit and 64 receive paths, an antenna setup designed to handle more traffic on the same airwaves.

SpaceX, in other words, is still the one designing and rolling out the network.

"We're excited to collaborate with Qualcomm Technologies and leverage their industry expertise and platform to accelerate our timeline to develop our base station end-to-end architecture," said Michael Nicolls, Starlink's senior vice president, in Qualcomm's release.

SpaceX has spent over a year buying the airwaves this network needs. It agreed to pay about $19.6 billion, in shares and payments on EchoStar's debt, for EchoStar licenses covering up to 65 MHz of spectrum, a deal it expects to close near the end of November 2027. And on Oct. 8, it agreed to buy a nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz airwaves, which SpaceX expects to own by the middle of next year.

On SpaceX's Oct. 20 call about third-quarter results, President Gwynne Shotwell said S-band airwaves should handle most of the traffic, while the 800 MHz spectrum is there "to basically penetrate buildings." But the carrier service is still a way off. Shotwell said SpaceX's short-term priority is flying its Mobile V2 satellites through 2027 and integrating its spectrum purchases to start service in early 2028.

Starlink Mobile's revenue shows up in SpaceX's enterprise and government sales, according to its latest quarterly filing. That line climbed 91% year over year to $2.1 billion in the third quarter. But SpaceX doesn't break out the mobile part, and the filing credits most of the line's growth to more aircraft activations.

Of course, it's all in the segment that already makes most of SpaceX's profit. Connectivity revenue climbed 69% year over year to $5.2 billion in the third quarter, a bit faster than its 66% growth in the second quarter. The segment's operating income almost doubled, up 99% to $2.4 billion. Its operating margin jumped to around 45%, up from about 38% in both the year-ago quarter and the second quarter. And connectivity made up about 85% of SpaceX's total operating income of $2.8 billion. SpaceX's artificial intelligence (AI) business, which it calls super intelligence, earned $431 million in operating income.

CEO Elon Musk said on the call that he sees "a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year in connectivity revenue." Connectivity is running at around $21 billion a year today, so that path would mean growing the segment many times over.

The cell sites also add to a big tab. Management expects fourth-quarter capital spending alone to land at $35 billion to $40 billion as more AI computing capacity comes online. And SpaceX hasn't said what the ground network will cost.

SpaceX's valuation is around $1.85 trillion now. Management sees $33 billion to $37 billion in revenue for the first quarter of 2027, and if the midpoint held for a full year, the stock would trade at around 13 times sales. I think that price already assumes years of fast growth -- and a phone network that might not bring in much revenue before 2028 arguably adds little to the next couple of years of it.

In the end, the Qualcomm deal makes Starlink Mobile's carrier plan more concrete. SpaceX now has deals for the airwaves, a supplier for its base stations, and a 2027 start date. It just doesn't have revenue from any of it yet.

I still see SpaceX stock as a hold at about $136, and this deal doesn't change that for me.

#3012. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3011. McDonald's: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

The margin story rests on a 98% franchised target, and whether baseline traffic can carry that model through 2028 is still open.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, McDonald's (MCD +6.53%) announced global comparable sales growth of 1.5% for the quarter. For long-term investors, customer visit frequency and menu pricing power remain critical factors for sustainable profit growth. Three things management said on the call stand out.

Management is testing new everyday affordable meal options across 40% of U.S. restaurants to address entry-level pricing. Fixing baseline guest traffic remains key for franchise profitability and store volume.

Specialty beverages are expanding across global markets to capture non-peak customer traffic. Orders containing these beverages generate check totals that are larger than the full-day average check.

Refranchising efforts in international operated markets (IOM, company-operated international stores) continue as the business aims for a 98% franchised portfolio by 2028. This asset-light model protects operating margins and capital efficiency.

Baseline guest traffic is turning positive heading into the fourth quarter following targeted promotional interventions. Management is watching pricing discipline and store execution across international markets.

The company maintains a vast global store footprint, strong brand equity, and unmatched supply chain scale. Future value depends on executing its multi-year growth plan, McDonald's > NEXT, through digital engagement and modern store remodels.

#3009. History Says This Is the Best Time of the Presidential Cycle To Invest. Could Wednesday's Rally Spark an Epic Bull Market?

Historically, stocks have soared in the third year of a presidential term.

Stocks soared on Wednesday as investors reacted to Democrats' sweeping win in the midterm elections.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished up 3.2%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%) gained 1.8%, and the Nasdaq Composite closed 1.4% higher.

The surge seemed to take Wall Street by surprise as stocks had initially fallen when results started to come in on fears of a data center backlash. However, by the time markets had opened on Wednesday, those fears seemed fully absorbed. While stocks with exposure to the AI infrastructure market fell on Wednesday, the rest of the market soared as investors cheered decisive results, President Trump's acceptance of his party's defeat, and a renewed potential for interest rates and inflation to come down, and for the war in Iran to end, bringing down oil prices.

Stocks tend to go up after an election as investors appreciate the degree of certainty that's been revealed, but Wednesday's gain was especially strong. Does it signal more to come? Historically, stocks perform particularly well during the third year of a presidential term.

Let's take a look at what history says about the current market cycle, and why it could be a great time to invest.

Historically, the third year of the four-year term is the strongest and most reliable period for the stock market. On average, the S&P 500 has gained 13.7% in the third year of the presidential cycle since 1980, and positive returns happen 78%-91% of the time, depending on the period that's cited.

According to the Presidential Election Cycle Theory, the midterm election often leads to economic stimulus as incumbent administrations typically look to improve the economy ahead of the next presidential election. Historically, the Federal Reserve has also been more accommodative during the third year, though that may happen in this cycle. Finally, Wall Street also prefers the sense of political certainty coming out of the midterm election.

From the week before the midterm to the end of the following year, a period of about 14 months, the S&P 500 has gained every time in the last 19 cycles, a remarkable streak, with an average gain of 20.3%.

In addition to the tailwind from this stage of the presidential cycle, stocks also look poised for further gains because investors, in particular, like a divided government, and with Democrats taking solid control of both houses of Congress and President Trump still in the White House, the government is clearly divided between both parties.

Wall Street prefers a divided government because it creates gridlock and makes it less likely that any extreme legislation passes. Investors also typically move back into stocks after the election as the risk of unsatisfying results has passed.

Finally, stocks tend to perform better from November through April than from May through October. There's no perfect explanation for that trend, but institutional investors tend to rebalance in the fourth quarter, corporate and holiday bonuses get put into the market, and tax-loss harvesting at the end of the year can also help. Alternatively, trading volumes tend to be lower in the summer when people go on vacations and aren't as plugged into the market.

Investors should keep in mind that these are just historical averages or trends, and that this historical pattern won't be able to overcome a black swan event or deeper, structural challenges, should they arrive.

However, the market's reaction on Wednesday bodes well for more gains. Though AI infrastructure stocks fell on worries about a data center slowdown, hyperscalers popped as investors bet that they would benefit from a slower AI expansion plan.

Nine out of 11 stock market sectors moved higher, with only energy and industrials falling. It's just one session, but stocks are off to a good start post-midterms, and the pieces are there for more gains.

#3007. Kon Knueppel leaves season debut with Hornets early with leg injury after offseason hamstring issue

Kon Knueppel's season debut with the Charlotte Hornets didn't go as planned Wednesday night. Knueppel, who had been dealing with a left a hamstring injury in recent weeks, left Charlotte's 114-104 loss to the Brooklyn Nets early due to what the team called a left leg injury. Further specifics are not yet known, but the Hornets quickly ruled him out.

It appeared as if Knueppel pulled up awkwardly while trying to handle the ball on the wing early in the contest. He dribbled the ball off his foot, and then started limping off the floor in significant discomfort.

He had three points and went 0-for-1 shooting from the field in his six minutes on the court at the Barclays Center.

The second-year sharpshooter had yet to play this season due to a strained left hamstring. Knueppel suffered the injury during "offseason on-court activity," the Hornets said in September. He sat out all of the preseason and the team's first eight games.

Last week, Knueppel was assigned to the team's G League affiliate in Greensboro, North Carolina, as part of his recovery. The 21-year-old was initially listed as probable for the Nets game before receiving an upgrade in status hours before tip-off.

Knueppel finished second in NBA Rookie of the Year balloting last season after challenging 2025 No. 1 overall draft pick and eventual winner Cooper Flagg by averaging 18.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists. Selected No. 4 overall out of Duke in the 2025 NBA Draft, he led the league by making 273 3-pointers, shooting 43% on 673 attempts.

He helped the Hornets improve to 44-38 and earn a spot in the NBA play-in tournament as the No. 9 seed, turning around from the league's third-worst record at 19-63 in 2024-25.

The Nets (2-6) surged ahead in the fourth quarter Wednesday night to grab the 10-point win. Michael Porter Jr. led the way with 26 points and 10 rebounds while shooting 8-of-17 from the field, and Julius Randle added 22 points.

Naz Reid led the Hornets with 28 points and nine rebounds in the loss, which was their fifth straight and dropped them to 3-6 on the season. Grayson Allen added 22 points off the bench, and Brandon Miller finished with 10 points while shooting 2-of-15 from the field.

While specifics of Knueppel's latest injury aren't yet known, losing him for any significant stretch would undoubtedly be a tough development for the Hornets as they get started this season. The team hasn't been to the playoffs in more than a decade, and a healthy Knueppel would be a huge part of that push.
